idea: Analyst onboarding curriculum licensed to boutique funds
pain: No structured training; juniors learn by osmosis
v1: A ten-module curriculum licensed to one fund
verdict: Good recurring shape and real leverage, but small funds hire juniors rarely.

why.distribution: 20-50 warm firms, and the buyer is the head of research she already knows.
why.demand: Inferred from her own experience of unstructured training; no fund has been asked to pay.
why.fmf: She was trained badly and then trained others - she knows exactly what the curriculum should contain.
why.revenue_structure: Annual firm licence renewing while juniors keep arriving.
why.defensibility: Content plus her name; training providers could copy the structure but not the credibility.
why.leverage: Written once, licensed repeatedly; occasional live sessions.
why.time_to_revenue: Building a credible curriculum first: 3-6 months.
why.tailwind: Junior hiring in asset management is flat to shrinking, and AI is reducing junior headcount.
why.ceiling: £12k x 17 firms = £204k, but boutiques hire juniors too rarely to buy this annually.

ceiling_arithmetic: £12k x 17 firm licences = £204k. The problem is renewal logic: a boutique hiring one junior every two years will not pay annually. Realistic: 6-8 firms = £70-95k.
carries: Real leverage, annual licence structure, and content only she can write with authority.
kills: The buyer's need is episodic, so annual renewal is hard to justify. AI is also shrinking junior cohorts.
test: Ask five heads of research how many juniors they hired last year and what training they gave them.
test_pass: Several describe a real gap and a training budget.
test_fail: They hire one every few years and train ad hoc.
